Alpha Parent Portal — case study
Product design case study

Bringing every parent closer to their child's day at school.

Alpha Education Network runs a student learning platform used by thousands of classrooms. Parents were left outside it — checking attendance through phone calls and homework through group chats. This is the design of the portal that changed that.

ClientAlpha Education Network
StudioSKONZS
RoleProduct & UI/UX Design
PlatformWeb portal
The context

One network, three very different people to design for.

Alpha Education Network already had a polished student app — sign-up, sign-in, a learning dashboard built for teenagers finding their footing. It worked, but it only spoke to one side of the classroom.

Parents were still relying on phone calls to the front office, paper diaries, and scattered WhatsApp groups to know whether their child made it to first period, finished last night's homework, or has a fee voucher due next week.

"The student app answers 'how am I doing.' The parent portal needed to answer a quieter, more anxious question — 'is my child okay, today, right now.'"
Ayesha
Working parent, two children on the network

Checks the app between meetings. Needs the most important thing — attendance, a due fee, an urgent notice — visible in one glance, not buried three taps deep.

Needs: a dashboard that leads with today, not a menu.
Rizwan
First-time parent on a school portal

Has never used a system like this before. Reads every label carefully and trusts the app more when it explains itself — what a voucher is, why a leave takes 24 hours to approve.

Needs: plain language, and a system that never surprises him.
Design principles

Three ideas that shaped every screen.

Rather than a long list of rules, the portal was held to three standards — checked against every flow before it shipped.

Today first

The dashboard opens on the next class, the closest deadline, the one unpaid voucher — never a wall of menu tiles a worried parent has to decode.

One shade of red, many meanings

Alpha's crimson does double duty — brand and alert. So it's used with restraint: reserved for what genuinely needs attention, never decoration.

Never a dead end

Every empty state, pending request and rejected leave application tells the parent what happens next, in the school's own voice.

The design system

A small solar system of decisions, all orbiting one identity.

Color, type, iconography and motion aren't separate choices — they're gravitationally bound to the same brand core, so the portal always feels like one product.

Why a system, not a style guide

Six teachers, a fee office and a principal's calendar all needed to live inside one app without clashing. Treating the pieces as orbits — not a checklist — kept the whole system legible even as new screens were added late in the project.

Core brand — signals and urgency
Supporting warmth — never alarms
Utility accents — status, fees, progress

The interface

Walking through the portal.

Thirteen core screens, grouped the way a parent actually moves through them — from the first sign-in to a leave request their child's teacher needs to see.

01

Getting in the door

A dark, confident sign-in sets the tone, then hands off to a warm registration flow and a simple way to attach every child on the account.

02

The home base

Everything a parent checks in the first ten seconds — attendance, grade, pending tasks, the next class and the next fee — sits above the fold.

Academics, made legible

Timetable, homework, attendance and exam reports share one visual language, so a parent who learns one screen already understands the rest.

Staying in the loop

Announcements read like a school newsletter, not a feed. Notifications separate what's urgent from what's routine, and let a parent tune each channel.

Details that matter

The small decisions a parent never notices — and would miss if they were gone.

01

Status colors are consistent everywhere

Green always means present or completed, amber always means pending, red always means overdue — in attendance, homework, fees and leave applications alike.

02

Multiple children, one mental model

Switching a child is one tap from any screen, and the app never asks a parent to re-orient — the same layout just carries new data.

03

Forms explain their own timing

The leave application tells a parent it's reviewed within 24 hours before they submit it, not after — so silence never reads as being ignored.

04

Notification preferences are granular

A parent can want a push alert for attendance but only a weekly digest for grades — the settings panel treats these as separate promises.

Reflection

A portal that earns a parent's trust one honest screen at a time.

The measure of this project was never how many features it shipped — it was whether a parent could open the app during a busy morning and know, immediately, that their child is okay. Every color, form and empty state was held to that bar.
